query: Consider the following context: Conventional material processing approaches often achieve strengthening of materials at the cost of reduced ductility. In that context, which method can be used for overcome the strength-ductility trade-off, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A data-driven machine learning approach that optimizes standard thermo-mechanical processing parameters can produce heterostructured architectures (e.g., gradient or bimodal phase distributions with coherent interfaces) in conventional alloys to simultaneously enhance strength and ductility, thereby overcoming the traditional trade-off.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional, homogeneously processed alloy that exhibits standard strength-ductility trade-offs, where typical strengthening methods (e.g., dislocation strengthening, grain refinement) yield high strength at the cost of reduced ductility.
generation.intervention: Implement a machine learning model that correlates processing parameters (e.g., thermal cycles, deformation schedules) with microstructural descriptors to design and control heterostructured architectures (e.g., gradient or bimodal structures with engineered soft/hard phase distributions).
generation.conditions: Standard processing and room-temperature tensile testing conditions under which conventional homogeneous alloys exhibit a trade-off between strength and ductility.
generation.structural_mediator: Engineered heterointerfaces in a gradient or bimodal microstructure, where coherent boundaries between softer and harder regions promote distributed plasticity.
generation.mechanism: The heterogeneous structure facilitates an inhomogeneous strain distribution by activating multiple deformation mechanisms at the phase interfaces, delaying crack initiation and enabling both high strength and enhanced ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline homogeneous microstructure, the ML-optimized heterostructured alloy will show a simultaneous improvement in both tensile strength and ductility, with the strength increase maintained or enhanced while ductility is improved by better strain distribution.
generation.baseline: Conventional alloy processing that yields a uniform microstructure with high strength but low ductility due to early crack initiation and localized strain concentration.
generation.boundary: This approach is limited to conventional processing routes and ambient testing conditions; the optimal processing parameters and microstructural configurations may vary with the alloy system and remain uncertain without extensive model training and validation.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty in precisely predicting the optimal processing parameters needed to achieve the desired heterostructuring, and the effect magnitude might depend on specific alloy compositions and processing nuances not fully captured by current ML models.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of conventional alloy samples: one set processed by standard methods producing homogeneous microstructure, and the other set processed using ML-optimized thermo-mechanical schedules aimed at inducing gradient or bimodal heterostructures. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests and perform detailed microstructural characterization (using SEM, TEM, and EBSD) to assess the phase distribution and interface coherence.
measurements: Tensile strength (ultimate tensile strength and yield strength)
Microstructural characterization (phase distribution, lamellar/gradient architectures, interface quality)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ML-optimized samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant simultaneous improvement in both tensile strength and ductility compared to the baseline homogeneous samples (i.e., if ductility is not improved or strength declines), then the hypothesis that ML-guided heterostructuring can overcome the strength–ductility trade-off is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] . decision.trend: Early work in high-entropy and refractory alloys initially pursued conventional compositional and processing modifications. The first paper showcased a lamellar microstructure in an EHEA that unexpectedly delivered both high strength and ductility. Later studies, by adjusting thermo‐mechanical treatments, demonstrated that tailoring phase distributions – for example by creating an 'inverted' microstructure or engineering multiple coherent precipitates – can delay damage onset and activate multiple deformation mechanisms. In essence, the trend has been moving away from homogeneous, uniformly processed alloys, towards exploiting microstructural heterogeneity (lamellar, bimodal, or gradient architectures) to decouple strength from ductility loss.
decision.unsolved: Despite these advances, it remains challenging to systematically design and control heterostructured architectures (such as gradient or bimodal structures) with conventional processing routes. The optimal processing parameters that yield the precise spatial distribution of phases or defects required to maximize both strength and ductility are still not fully understood or predicted.
decision.lever: Implementing a data-driven model that correlates processing parameters (e.g., thermal cycles, deformation schedules) and microstructural descriptors (e.g., phase gradient profiles, dispersion of lamellae/precipitates) with mechanical performance.
decision.why: Given the historical shift towards engineering microstructural heterogeneity to overcome the strength–ductility trade-off, a machine learning approach is a natural next step. It will enable the efficient exploration and optimization of complex processing–structure–property relationships that were previously determined by trial-and-error. This approach directly addresses the unsolved challenge of predicting and controlling heterostructured architectures under conventional processing conditions.
